title: Smart home
like: lights and locks controlled from a phone
brief: One million homes have a hub that keeps a live connection to your cloud. The hub reports its devices every few minutes, and the phone app sends commands like "lock the door". Commands must feel instant and must not be repeated. Once in a while a power cut ends and every hub reconnects together.

clarify.q: How fast must a command feel?
clarify.a: A tap on the phone should switch the light in under a third of a second most of the time.

clarify.q: What if a command arrives twice?
clarify.a: A lock command twice is usually harmless, but "toggle the garage door" twice is not. Treat commands as one-time actions.

clarify.q: What happens if a whole region goes down?
clarify.a: Homes should connect to the other region within a couple of minutes, and commands should work again.

clarify.q: How many users are in Europe?
clarify.a: About a third. The rest are mostly in North America.

requirements.users: 1 million homes and 2.5 million app users (approx.)
notes: Each hub sends a batch of device states every few minutes.
A hub holds one open connection. A single gateway node holds about 100,000 connections.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

numbers.label: Gateway nodes to hold 1 million hub connections at 100,000 each
Device batches per second at peak

hints: A hub keeps a connection open all day. What holds a million open connections without becoming the thing that breaks?
A socket gateway layer holds the connections and passes messages inward. For a region outage, route users with geo DNS and keep a copy of hub state in a second region.
Reconciliation is bounded state recovery, not blind action replay. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: This problem is about connections, not requests per second. A million open sockets need a layer of their own. The other lesson is to treat commands as actions that happen once, and to expect that after a power cut, a million hubs call home in the same minute.

designs.name: Two regions, connection layer in front
designs.why: A socket gateway layer in each region holds the open connections. Device state sits in a key-value store that is cheap per write at this volume. Geo DNS sends hubs to the nearest healthy region, and the idempotency store makes a repeated command harmless.

designs.name: One serving region with active recovery
designs.why: The second region mirrors every required service and can take over in about 30 seconds. This costs more than a cold standby but meets the stated short recovery window.

tradeoffs: A second region costs about a third more and turns a region outage from hours of downtime into a short reconnect.
A key-value table is cheap per write and cannot answer complex questions. Keep a separate reporting copy for those.
Jittered reconnect spreads a million hubs over a minute or two, at the price of some hubs waiting a bit to get back online.
Treating commands as one-time actions needs an idempotency key on every command, and removes a whole class of rare bugs.
A cold standby is cheap and slow. A warm standby is faster and costs closer to a second region.
editorial.realWorld: Smart-home clouds keep hundreds of thousands of connections per gateway node and ask devices to reconnect with random delays after an outage (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Smart home: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Deliver commands once with bounded validity across reconnects. Device-side deduplication protects the physical action, not just the cloud request. A stale physical command can be dangerous; delivery and validity are different promises. Reconciliation is bounded state recovery, not blind action replay.

fields.label: Step 1. Door command C is acknowledged by the hub but cloud loses the reply. Retry how?
options: Reuse C and return its durable execution result
fields.explanation: Device-side deduplication protects the physical action, not just the cloud request.

fields.label: Step 2. An hour-old unlock command is still queued after reconnection. Execute it?
options: Replay every queued command to avoid loss
Reject it after its explicit validity deadline
fields.explanation: A stale physical command can be dangerous; delivery and validity are different promises.

fields.label: Step 3. All hubs reconnect after a power cut. What restores state?
options: Jittered reconnects, authenticated sessions and versioned desired versus observed state
fields.explanation: Reconciliation is bounded state recovery, not blind action replay.

correctness.responsibility: Deliver commands once with bounded validity across reconnects.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
